summary: A definition of the Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol from the Network Graphics Working Group, written by Ira Cotton of MITRE. All input is described by type, origin and length followed by the data. Level 0 defines two input types, text and simple position, and lists device codes such as keyboard, tablet, mouse and lightpen.

eli5.summary: When you click or type on a drawing screen, the computer needs a way to tell the other computer what happened. This sets simple rules: say what kind of thing it was, where it came from, and how big it is.

questions: how does ngp-0 send text and position input
what are the input types in rfc 336
subtitle: A protocol for how input devices send information to graphics systems.

tldr.problem: Graphics systems need a standard way to communicate input from devices like keyboards, mice and tablets over the network.
tldr.mechanism: Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol defines a simple format: each input is described by a type code, a device code, a length, and then the actual data.
tldr.outcome: Two input types are defined: text (from keyboards, joysticks and other text sources) and simple position (mouse or tablet coordinates as signed fractions).

today: RFC 336 describes a graphics input protocol designed in 1972 for the early ARPANET. It is marked Unknown status and defines only the most basic input types; later levels and later graphics protocols superseded it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 336 defines the Level 0 Graphic Input Protocol, created by the Network Graphics Working Group. The protocol is a simple way to describe input from devices connected to a graphics system. Drawing programs and remote graphics systems need a standard format to understand what a user did: typed text, clicked a button, or moved a stylus.

The protocol uses a consistent structure: every input is described by a type code (what kind of input), an origin code (which device sent it), a length (how many bytes follow), and then the actual data. This simple three-part header makes the protocol easy to parse and extend.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending a postcard that always has the same format: first say what you drew or wrote, then say where you drew it with, then the actual picture or text. Any mail carrier can handle it.

sections.title: Two Input Types
sections.content:
Level 0 defines exactly two kinds of input: text and simple position (coordinates). Text input uses type code 1 and sends keyboard characters in network ASCII. Simple position input uses type code 2 and sends x and y coordinates as signed fractions (always 4 bytes total at this level).

Each input also includes a device code to identify where it came from. Defined devices are: primary keyboard, tablet, mouse, joystick, lightpen, cursor controls, keyset, and combined mouse-keyset. Device code 0 marks an unspecified device when the source is unknown.
sections.eli5: The protocol handles two things: words (text from a keyboard) and locations (where you touched with a mouse or stylus). Each message also says which tool made the input, like keyboard or mouse.

sections.title: Format Details
sections.content:
A text input message is formatted as: TEXTIN:DEVICE:COUNT:Text String. TEXTIN is code 1; DEVICE is the device code; COUNT is the number of bytes in the text string; the text follows in network ASCII format.

A position input message is formatted as: POSIT:DEVICE:COUNT:x:y. POSIT is code 2; DEVICE is the device code; COUNT is the total byte count for both coordinates (4 bytes at Level 0); x and y are signed fractions.

Data that does not fit this format should be sent on a separate connection rather than through the graphics input link, to avoid protocol overhead.
sections.eli5: Text messages put the type, device, count and text in order. Position messages put the type, device, count and the two coordinates in order. If something does not fit, use a different channel.

fields.name: Device Code
fields.desc: 0 unspecified, 1 keyboard, 2 tablet, 3 mouse, 4 joystick, 5 lightpen, 6 cursor, 7 keyset, 8 mouse-keyset

references.text: Crocker, D., "Network Graphic Attention Handling", RFC 178, June 1971.
